4/4/2024 Spanky Training/Handling Tips:? Drop off enrichment to help him expend some mental energy if possible before taking him out. (Frozen enrichment can be found in the white freezer located in the back sally port)? Before opening the kennel, show him your treats and ask him to “sit” and then give him a treat when he sits. If he’s excited, it  may take a few asks before he responds. Then use the treat on the other side of the loop trick to get the leash on him.? Keep treats visible as you walk and throw them on the ground for him to “find it” until you get outside or he shifts his attention to his surroundings ? If he bites at the leash, continue walking while ignoring the behavior. If you are in a contained area, intersperse dropping the leash in response to any increase in tugging. As soon as there is a slight pause or decrease in intensity, redirect him with “down” and/or “sit” and then give him a treat with verbal praise. Repeat as needed.? Start walking again, a treat + praise or throwing treat for him to "find it" every few steps ? If he starts to bite again, correct him by saying “eh” and then reset his behavior with “down” or “sit” followed by treat + praise. Then resume walking ? Once biting stops, keep him engaged and reinforce good walking with intermittent treats thrown for him to find? When un/re-leashing, first ask him to “sit” first and then give him a treat.  ** If you try to pull the leash away from him, he will tug back. If you ignore, drop the leash (he's not a runner), and redirect him with a command, then he will drop the leash to fetch the treat! ** Continue asking him to "find it" until he is leading the walk and no longer looking at you. At this point, he'll be easy on leash ** Any time you need to adjust/tighten/handle the leash, ask him to do something and reward him right as you do it (this results in him focusing on what you want him to do vs. the leash you're adjusting)

Work on distance, distraction and duration as three separate levels of difficulty. See below a list of activities you can do to help Theo with his reactivity and also to meet strangers.Confidence:Sniffing GamesFind it! This is a great game to play encouraging your dog to find a treat (or toy if he has a favorite toy). Show your dog a treat or his favorite toy, and then place it out of his sight but easily accessible. Tell him to “Find it!”. Once he finds it praise enthusiastically. You can start to increase the difficulty of the game by turning off the lights, adding more treats, using boxes or even hiding treats in less conventional places like inside of a shoe. The rewards for the dog are multiple- he gets a treat or finds his toy plus a very happy handler. If issuing a toy, be sure to reward his find with some play before starting again. When multiple treats or toys are used, this particular game helps to build persistence and trust in the handler. The dog may initially find only 2 out of 3 treats, but he quickly discovers that persistence in searching when you give the “Find it!” cue pays off. He learns to believe you - there really is another one there! FreeworkIntroduction to FreeworkPlace snuffle mats and licky mats around an rea of your hours and load them with treats, yogurt, peanut butter, etc… Let your dog go in and explore the area while enjoying the amazing treats you set out for him. Don’t give him big pieces, this activity is more about the journey of finding the treats. Try using small crumbs so encourage more sniffing. You can also use your dog’s kibble for this. This game allows your dog to freely go in an area and explore. You can also do the same set-up outdoors to encourage him to sniff in situations where he might want to bark otherwise. Scatter FeedScatter Feeding Dogs: A Step-by-Step Guide To Our Favourite Calm Enrichment Activity!Why scatter feeding is beneficial for dogsScatter feeding provides a way for Theo to use his nose and calm down. You can use the same cue as “Find it!”. Do this in your back yard or even Sniffspots! Consent TestPetting Consent Tests movieParticing this form of consent testing will help Theo have some predictability when meeting strangers. Knowing that he wont be petted unless requested can be very empowering for dogs. When Theo meets strangers, please encourage your visitors to not do strong eye contact or talk to Theo at least initially. Let Theo do some freework or scatter feet for some minutes while he is adjusting to the presence of the new visitor. Communication:Teach Unprompted Attention/Auto Check-InAuto Check-In.pdfI am attaching a handout on how to do this but here is a short course on how to teach it with some demo videos: https://suzanneclothier.com/shop/autocheckin/This is very similar to the “Look at me” cue with the difference that it’s coming from the inside out where the dog is voluntarily offering attention. Puppy Politeness PokerPractice Puppy Politeness Poker by creating a list of reliable cues Theo will enthusiastically perform. Also create a list of real-life rewards that he will work for (meal time, access to a snuffle mat, opening a door, etc). Utilize those cues to give him explicit permission to access something he wants and change it up every time. This will teach Theo to slow down, listen to your request and work for what he wants. Teaches impulse control, attention and it polishes the communication between you and him. You can learn more about this concept by watching this free webinar: https://suzanneclothier.com/member_video_library/puppy-politeness-poker-webinar/Training:Teaching TouchTouch.pdfOnce Theo is able to give a “Touch” when cued in different situations, you can start using this cue during walks when you see that he spots an other dog and want to prevent him from reacting. You might need to use smellier rewards in the beginning. Practice WaitI don’t have a hand-out for wait but it sounds like Theo already knows this behavior and he just need to practice. Start small with baby steps. Take one step at a time to build distance. Once you are able to ask Theo to wait and go to a different room you can start working on duration. Once Theo is able to wait for a longer period of time you can throw in distractions like maybe closing a door and then opening it. The more you practice this, the easier it will be for him once you take it outside and introduce it in the stairs. Remember to start out with baby steps, even through Theo already has mastered “Wait” with distance, duration and distractions in-doors, you still want to start with just one step outdoors. Management:Teach 1-2-3 Treat! https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ui6dWBDdDScI wasn’t able to find any great videos of this (I should make my own lol) but basically you condition your dog to expect a treat when they hear the word “three”. If you practice this in-doors with no distractions, you eventually will be abe to do this outdoors. When you see another dog coming then you can perform the pattern that Theo already knows and he will prefer to be next to you waiting for the treat instead of reacting to the other dog. Emergency “U” turnTeaching an Emergency U Turn Portland Dog Training/ Teach an Emergency U-Turn for your Reactive Dog/ Noble Woof Dog TrainingTeaching Theo an Emergency “U” turn will help you get out of situations where he is likely to react. By practicing this, you will be able to prevent him from practicing the undesirable behavior. Scatter FeedAfter Theo has had a lot of practice with the “Find it” cue, you can do a scatter feed during walks when you see there is a dog approaching on the opposite site of the street. Please be mindful that this would be done if you are sure that the other dog is not walking towards you or wont approach you. This is meant as a management technique to prevent him from reacting to an other dog and rehearse the undesirable behavior. TouchOnce Theo learns touch, you can also do this to basically step aside and call him over buy asking him to touch. This will allow you to position him an a way where he is not facing the other dog approaching and will buy you some time while the other dog finishes crossing. Follow up:I recommend booking an in-person appointment to work on counter conditioning and desensitizing Theo to other dogs during walks and address reactivity issues. Additionally we can work practicing polite greetings with strangers. To book your next in-person appointment please visit https://loyalpawrenting.pet/ → Book Now → First Let’s Meet → Step 2: In-Home Assessment.During this 1.5 hr visit, we will work on creating a customized training, enrichment and management plan to set up Theo for success. We will also perform a Relationship Assessment Test to determine behavior patterns in your relationship with Theo. If you are interested in self-paced training I recommend taking the following course by Victoria Stillwell: https://positively.com/learning/course/help-stop-reactivity

I knelt down to his level and offered treats. He was not interested in my treats and instead he got so nervous he urinated. I sat on the ground with my back facing away from him and allowed him to get familiar with my presence. He would occasionally come up to the gate to see what I was doing but then immediately retracted to the back of the kennel. He would low growl with whale eyes if I turned around. Realizing that he was more scared then anything, I cracked the run door open to see if he would approach. As soon as the run door opened and I offered my hand for a sniff, he approached me with a low-wagging tail. I offered him my leash to which he lowered his head and allowed me to put it on. Exited the kennel and walked to the mulch yard. When we got into the mulch yard, I let him roam around (with the leash still on). I sat on the bench and allowed him to approach me if he wanted. I observed that he was heavily panting due to stress. However, he would approach me with a wagging tail and allow me to pet his head and back. We left the mulch yard and went for a walk to the next yard over where he did a fence greeting with Bubba Boy. He seemed excited to meet another dog and I suspect he is dog friendly. We then walked inside and I brought him over to the supervisor desk. He stopped midway to greet two customers in which he offered submissive ears and a tail wag. Once at the desk, he was met by a few kennel techs. While he did show some shyness, he allowed one kennel tech to pet his head. We went back to 200, I placed him back in his kennel and unleashed without incident. Recommend L3-SF and a playgroup assessment.

I removed the leash with no issues, closed the kennel door and slide another treat to him. 8/21/2025 8/21/25Hi there,Here are notes about Whiskey during this week-long evaluation.  We can keep him for a few more days, possibly returning him on Sunday or Monday - still working on the logistics as we will be traveling next week and I know Tuesdays are rough and I want to continue to set him up for success as much as possible.Home set-up:Whiskey was housed in a separate room, away from our 2 resident dogs.  The room is double gated at the door - a baby gate at the threshold and a removable gate to add more distance from my resident dog's noisy eyes to the entrance of the room.  The room is on the third floor of our townhome and was set-up with cameras for additional monitoring.  The loudest the room would get would be when I was home and on work calls.  We also had an air filter running all day, on it's highest setting it can be loud, but seemed like white noise.When Whiskey needed to go out/downstairs for a walk or to go potty, our 2 residents dogs were crated and secured in a space on the main floor where Whiskey could not approach their gates directly.  The ground floor is my husband's space and where he works.  We practiced crate and rotate in our home while Whiskey was with us.Daily routine:Whiskey was taken out 3-4 times a day, depending if I went to the office.  Frequent breaks ensured he did not go potty in the house.  When at home, one of those outings would be a lunch-time or early afternoon 10-15 minute walk outside.  Whiskey was fed 2x a day, breakfast and dinner.  When working from home, I would crate him after breakfast and after his lunch-time walk, I would have him roam the room free while I continued to work. After dinner, I let Whiskey have the room on his own, uncrated.  He usually just lay on the floor and watched the door until I came back.  He would be crated overnight as he slept.Health notes:Whiskey still coughs, but there are no signs of phlegm and his nose is no longer runny/mucus-y.  His coughs happen mostly when he has just woken up or when he's walking up and down the stairs.  He is still taking doxy in the AM along with his breakfast.  He is still butt scoots on occasion.  His nose and paws are very dry though, they feel scratchy. Pus still continues to show up around his eyes, though not as much as when he first got here - but still present.  He seems to have some stiffness in his rear legs though.Eyesight:I think Whiskey can see shadows, the bigger the item the better he can maneuver around it or at least know that it's there.  He still walks down steps tentatively, but I've noticed that he prefers to walk along the stair wall, I'm assuming it helps him navigate.  He also seems to navigate better in bright light vs. a dark room.I don't know if it's eyesight or spatial distancing might be his issue or both, but sometimes he will run right into me in the backyard because he didn't realize I was right there.  He often missteps when coming to a curb. He may also flinch when you pet him on the head or under his chin because he didn't see your hand coming.General behavior:Talking - When he does make a sound, he roos or makes deep vocal grunts.  It can sound growly, but as you get to know him, it's not a growl or at least not a warning one.  He's usually vocal when we are outside or when I'm with him upstairs and playing with him and his toys.On-leash - He can pull, but he's getting better at not pulling too hard.  When he pulls, it's because something got his attention, curiosity, or interest.  Dogs walking (or barking), people walking by, strollers nearby, cats, etc.Leash-biting - Only showed leash biting when we swapped leash to a slip lead vs. leash with a clasp to his collar.  He initially attempted leash biting when you try to put the slip lead over his head. If you dangle the other end of the leash in front of him, he has tried to grab it.  To curb this, we've sprayed the slip lead with bitter apple spray and also use special treats to reward him when we can put on/take off the leash with minimal to none LB behavior.  We have also rewarded him when he lets go of the leash, if he was able to get a hold of it.  I have noticed that when the slip lead is loop is big enough where it can go over his head without him touching it on the sides of his face, it is easier and quicker to get the leash on.Potty-trained:  Whiskey is potty-trained, though it may take a few days for him to learn where he can go.  We aim to have him go out 4x a day to prevent any accidents, though 3x a day can also work where he was taken out in the morning, when I got home from work, and before going to bed.Crate-trained:  Whiskey does well in a crate and has learned to go inside on his own by tapping on the top of the crate.  Since the time he's been with us, he's only barked once in the crate, and that was during a thunderstorm. He only barked once and then was able to settle.  As he got healthier/felt safer, he midly whines when he is in the crate but still sees you near. It's more of a muffled whine, but he does not do it long and then just lays down in the crate to sleep.Treats - Whiskey is a gentle treat taker, because of his sight issues, he may need a visual cue to listen to where the treat is.  The best treats for him are smelly ones.Interactions:Other people in the home/men:  He has responded well to my husband who has given Whiskey pets and treats. My husband would come up to the baby gate where Whiskey would come up and seek pets.  Whiskey would also go up to my husband on his own when my husband was at his desk to seek pets.Kids:  We have not had him directly near kids or interact with kids.  The closest to a kid he has been was walking by the community pool on a weekend.  These were mostly small/younger kids, but a few were screaming very loudly that it made Whiskey anxious.  He pulled me towards the pool gate and attempted to try to put his head through the fence. I'm not sure if he had the intention to go through the fence or if he just couldn't tell/see a fence existed.Cats: We bumped into a neighborhood cat who was more scared of  Whiskey than Whiskey was of the cat.  Whiskey showed some interest, but I was able to call him towards me before we continued our walk.Dogs:  Both resident dogs seem curious about Whiskey, but we did not allow any type of meet and greet or walks together.  Reese (our female dog) would watch him through the baby gate+secondary gate.  When he knows she's there he will go over to the doorway.  On the second day, it seemed like he was about to make an attempt to jump on the baby gate to get a better look at Reese, but I told him "no" and got him to go back into his crate.  He hasn't tried it since.Toys and things:  Whiskey seems to prefer crinkly type toys the best, though eh has been caught licking or mouthing at sheets/towels we used to catch any potty accidents.  He's not tearing or destroying anything, just lightly mouthing/nibbling.Suggestions:If Whiskey is unable to find placement out of the shelter, it's unclear if he will regress/decline once he's back at the shelter. Considering his stressors, this could be highlly likely.  If possible, he may do well in one of the flex rooms as they have more room and tend to be a lot quieter than the runs.

Parcel ended up with some respiratory issues and was fixed so he has spent most of his time quarantined from out other pets. This has also meant that we have not gotten out to do a lot of things that we would have at this point. I would like to update this after he gets to fully integrate in a few weeks. Parcel is an even tempered happy go lucky guy. He is pretty chill most of the time and will go with the flow. He enjoys being around and playing with other dogs, fine being around cats, curious, wants to be friends, just not sure how. Most of all, he really craves human attention. He will jump and be a bit mouthy at times when he really wants attention, but we are working on this. He is incredibly gentile taking treats, not a food or treat aggressive, fully crate trained, does well on a leash and loves to go on walks, he enjoys being outside in the back yard, but does not want to be left out on his own, rides well in the car, likes all people and is happy to get attention.Daily Routine He goes outside to the bathroom first thing, then eats and out again before a short walk in the morning. I will let him out a few times during the day as he is not fully housebroken. Around dinner time he gets fed again and will go out to do his business immediately after he eats. He goes on a second longer walk in the afternoon/evening.What food do they eat? Dry dog food and treats.What would be an ideal home and family for your foster? A family with time to give him lots of attention. I think he really likes having a "big brother" and some cat siblings and would do fine in a house with other pets, but he would also be happy to get all of the attention. After he recovers, we will spend time out hiking some of the local parks and see what he thinks about that and his energy level. My current dog never stops.On a scale of 1 to 5 how housetrained are they? 3Does your foster use a kennel without excessive barking/whining, escape attempts, or destruction? Fully crate trained. He may whine very briefly when you walk away, but does not bark or act out. He will willingly go in the crate when asked.Where do they sleep at night? However, I think he would be very happy to sleep with the rest of us.Do they sleep through the night? YesHas he / she been exposed to any kids? If yes, what ages? How did it go? Yes, we have 3 cats and his initial engagements were very positive. Parcel was mildly curious, but did not chase or even become excited. Of course, this is the same dog that does not chase squirrels. I'm not sure he is really a dog! (just kidding).Do they prefer men or women? No preferenceDoes he / she live with another dog? Yes, I have a 67 lb mix. They were very happy to play. 3/4/2025 Foster reached out to me with the following message:Hey Fina, I have a behavior question for you regarding Whiskey. He went on trial adoption, but was returned to me after 4 days. They said he was too high energy and didn’t settle well in the evening, even though they felt like they had given him plenty of exercise. Their backyard set up ended up not being great because the fence wasn’t good and the dog Nextdoor was out and barked non stop. So when they walked him on their busy street, he got overstimulated. I think he didn’t have any time to really decompress there (he took a few day when he first came to me) and he never really settled in. They shared their concern about him barking and growling at them and “throwing a tantrum” when he didn’t get what he wanted, for example if he wanted to play while they were sitting on the couch. I’ve had him bark at me before in a play bow and try to jump up and get mouthy to elicit play or attention, but I have redirected him to a toy or left the room and the behavior stopped. I did tell them during the meet and greet about his mouthiness at times and the leash biting when overstimulated which has gotten much better, but it seems as this behavior came when he was frustrated with not getting something he wanted. I just got him back late last night and he is settling back in pretty well, but I’m wondering what I should do if this behavior continues. Any help would be appreciated! Thanks,Emily My email back:Hi Emily,I'm so sorry to hear that Whiskey's trial adoption didn’t work out. Please don’t feel discouraged—four days is not enough time for Whiskey to decompress, learn his new routine, and bond with new people.Sometimes, exercise doesn’t actually tire dogs out; instead, it can be like adding fuel to the fire. Have you ever taken a gym class, only to feel even more energized afterward and want to keep going? Exercise can have that same effect on both people and dogs. There could be many reasons why Whiskey had a hard time settling—it sounds like the combination of new people, a new environment, a barking dog, and a busy street may have overwhelmed him.The phrase "throwing a tantrum" concerns me. Whiskey isn’t trying to give them a hard time; he’s having a hard time and expressing his emotions the only way he knows how. Unfortunately, it can be difficult to get people to understand that behavior is just behavior—not evidence of dogs plotting against us (lol).I think ACE Freework could be really beneficial for Whiskey. This involves using snuffle mats and licking mats to encourage dogs to explore and engage their noses, which helps them calm down. Regularly practicing this will not only boost Whiskey’s confidence but also provide him with a safe space to explore without any pressure or expectations. The next family he visits can then use the same items in their home, offering Whiskey a sense of predictability and normalcy during the transition. I have a bit more information in this video: https://youtu.be/b1pImAsxRlw?si=aqITiFXnasrLmxLy. You can try some of the activities I mention and encourage the next family to do the same with Whiskey. For future placements, I also recommend that the next family have some frozen Kongs on hand. That way, if they’re relaxing on the couch and Whiskey wants to play, they can redirect him to a frozen Kong or a long-lasting chew while they unwind.I hope this is helpful! Please let me know how things go.Best regards,Fina Garcia

10/26/2023 10/25/23 I took Marty and my two dogs out to the yard. We have been keeping my one dog that he previously got into a fight with a Marty separate, but they have been doing better. So I took them outside and kept Marty on a leash in the yard to help him stay calm and work on boundaries. Everything was going well. Then someone I do not know parked in front of the fence and a large lab put its head out of the window and started barking in a bit of an aggressive way. My dogs reacted and ran up to the fence and started barking back. The owner then got out of the car and put the dog on a leash and brought it up to the fence. The lab dog was barking aggressively at my dogs, and they were getting very agitated. I kept Marty at a distance since he was on the leash. I called out to her and asked her to move away from the fence. She didn't really respond, and she looked like she was going to open the gate to come in. I then became scared she was going to enter, and I don't think she lives here so maybe she did not know the rules. I moved closer to try to get my dogs away from the fence. In his agitation my dog turned around and went for Marty and that is when they started fighting. I tried to get them apart, but they had latched onto each other's faces and wouldn't let go. A neighbor saw what was happening and he came into the yard and was trying to help me separate them. He managed to reach in and pull Marty's head back, but my dog was still trying to get to him. I think Marty was scared and in all the chaos he bit my neighbor's arm. I don't believe Marty intentionally bit my neighbor but was just in fight or flight mode. My neighbor went to the hospital, and I did get in contact, and they said the hospital notified animal control. I provided the vaccine records for both dogs. I asked for pictures of the injury, but they have not provided them so far. I was a bit alarmed to find out that Marty's rabies shots were not up to date. I am afraid that could put me in a very bad situation where I could face legal issues. If she is consistently performing auto check-ins in distracting environments, she is ready to move to the next phase! when she does the auto check-in, say, "You are so good." (It doesn’t have to be this exact phrase, but choose a four-word phrase that’s not too long and be consistent in using it.) When she does the auto check-in, say the phrase slowly, and if, by the end of the sentence, she is still maintaining direct eye contact, you can ask her to do an easy task like touch, sit, or spin—choose something she already knows and enjoys doing. If you're unable to finish the phrase before she looks away, that’s okay! It just means you need to continue reinforcing the auto check-in a bit longer. Don’t forget to give her small treats one at a time for 5–15 seconds while you verbally praise her for the auto check-in.Regarding the meet-and-greets, doing it in your patio is a great idea! As mentioned, there’s no exact formula, and you may need to pivot depending on her body language, but your plan sounds solid. :) You might want to be prepared with a snuffle mat and consider having guests come in one at a time so it’s not overwhelming with too many new people at once. She can explore around them, maybe sniff a little, but she also has the option to engage with the snuffle mats, alternating between checking the family out and using the mats. 12/30/2024 I was asked to send both DCAS and FCAS an email together about an altercation that we had today between our foster dogs. We introduced FCAS Zena to DCAS Dimple today - we have had both for 2 weeks but Dimple was in quarantine so they haven't met yet. We gave Zena 100mg trazodone before the meeting.We were told by Zena's previous foster that Zena does better with intros without a leash, so we first kept them on leash, but eventually dropped Zena's leash in our backyard. We tried to keep them from getting too much face-to-face time, but let them sniff and petted them both so they could get smells without getting face to face. After a couple minutes Zena lashed out at Dimple, jumping on her back and biting her on the neck. My husband pulled Zena off Dimple within a couple seconds. There was no evidence of injury to Dimple at that point.We then went for a parallel walk - after a couple minutes, Zena stopped being that interested and they kept to themselves on the walk for about 20 min. WE got back and again tried to drop Zena's leash. Zena was being good and keeping her distance - coming closer at times but then backing off. But then Zena charged, jumped on Dimple's back, and bit her again. We were able to break them up swiftly again, however Dimple has 3 bite/scratch marks on the left side of her face/head.Since that second incident they have been physically separated in different rooms. We're taking Dimple to DCAS later to get her cleaned up and looked at and we have multiple calls scheduled for behavioral consults - one with FCAS on Jan 7th. We were told to keep them apart for 2 more weeks but this isn't going to be easy.They are both dog friendly, but maybe Zena is better classified as dog selective. We had a temp foster for the last nine days, and Zena got on well with the temp foster. The temp foster was submissive whereas Dimple isn't.

I am sorry that I did not get the volunteers' names.  Both were white girls.  One was the same person who was in the exam room when I brought CP in on Sunday-- she has long, curly, light brown hair and was wearing tall rubber boots.  And the other volunteer that I spoke with has multiple piercings, light brown hair and a shag haircut and glasses.  Both girls were very knowledgable and professional-- took the time to speak to me at length.Here's a summary of what I told them.  Some of this did not seem to be in the record, but perhaps should be:- I called Fulton County Animal Control around 6pm on Wednesday 9/25 to report a dog barking and wimpering that was tied to a fence.  It is a wooden fence that surrounds apartments (The Grant, owned by Braden Fellman) that are behind my house.  - I didn't know it at the time, but a female tenant of the apartments had also called Animal Control to report the same dog that day- Thursday morning (9/26), Animal Control had still not shown up yet, so I went over to the apartments to investigate more closely myself. By chance, I met the lady who had also called animal control in the yard of the apartments and we both walked more closely to the barking dog to see what its condition was- there were about 3 men across from the dog, outside of the apartments.  I asked them if anyone owned the dog.  They all said no, didn't know who owned it.  -CP was barking and straining on the leash tied to the fence and seemed upset.  I suggested we wait for Animal Control and not approach the dog.  One of the men decided to walk over and undo CP's leash from the fence.  I thought this was brave.  CP seemed to want to go toward his apartment (I didn't think much about this at the time).  But, he handed the leash to me.  I was surprised and the details are a little blurry.  He asked me what I was going to do with the dog.  I said I was going to take her to the shelter and maybe foster it--  I took the leash and walked her back to my house. -Animal Control showed up later that morning, and the female tenant that I had met in the yard directed the AC agent to my house to see/record the dog.-I told animal control not to take the dog because I would take it to Lifeline and potentially try to foster it.  The animal control person entered the dog into the system as "Miracle."- I also told the volunteers about the party/shooting/potential link to party host's eviction/dog-handoff that my have happened to CP before I got her and brought her to Lifeline (noted in my initial email to you).I think that pretty much covers all that I know.  I hope it helps provide more context, better records, and explain her behavior.  I also showed the volunteers the photos and videos of CP contentedly gnawing on a bone, being obedient (she seemed like she knows "sit" and "come"), and going for a  walk calmly during the time that I had her.  She also enjoyed her shoulders being rubbed. Thanks again for your time here and for taking the time to capture this dog's story accurately. I gave one of the volunteers tonight my phone #, email contact, and address, in case you have any further questions about this or need more details.  I'll still plan to follow up on Wednesday to check in..  Hopefully CP is calming down.Thank you kindly,Jami

10/1/2024 From Foster:  Good morning,I’m following up on the behavior consult we signed up for in regards to Marvelous Mary’s reactivity to men. Our previous one got canceled due to storm preparations at the old shelter so I rescheduled for 9:30am today. Not sure if maybe it got missed but I didn’t get a call and I wanted to stress the importance of addressing this issue below, with the hopes of getting the needed advice/help.While she is a wonderful dog to me and my wife, and frankly great with any of our female friends and children, she is unpredictable around men. She lives in a female only household so this is not cause for concern at home. However, when we visited my parents-in-law there were a couple of instances, alongside a most recent instance, where she was completely fine one minute and then the next she snapped.The first instance where we determined she didn’t like men was when she was outside on a leash and my uncle, a potential adopter who wanted to meet her, tried to come near her. She was good for about 10 seconds, wagging her tail, being sweet, and then just started barking at him and trying to get close to him. He is older so she wasn’t able to get near him to do anything, and we thought maybe because he is so tall and had a long beard and a hat that she just didn't like that?*The next instance was when we had her meet the rest of the family, my nephews (3 and 12), my sister in law (20) and my brother in law (21), my mother in law (55) and my father in law (54). I was right next to her tied to a tree for that first encounter. We warned my brother in law that we don’t think she likes men and to be careful. To our initial surprise, she was completely fine, let him walk her around, allowed him to give her treats and pet her, and it was a non issue. She was great with the two kids, although backing away/skittish if they were screaming. Also great with my sister and mother in law (she doesn’t really like dogs but was convinced by Mary’s cuteness and general behavior inside the house). *So 30 minutes pass by and we’re all in the living room except for my brother in law. He walks past us/Mary, also wearing a hat and having a beard, and Mary jumps up, stalks him for a second, and then tries to nip the back of his leg. He jumps and we immediately recall her, which she comes without fuss. From then I had her on leash inside and I was a little stressed/nervous about the situation so I took her outside. *Again I tied her to the same tree (me sitting by her) by the garage where people would walk by. My brother in law was going to his car and she completely loses it with him going by. Barking aggressively no matter how far/close he was to her. Time passes by, all the women and kids are fine to touch her/get close to her, she's wagging her tail as I pet her. I told my brother in law to get a spoon with peanut butter on it. Maybe we can get her to be desensitized to the fact that he is a man and being friendly can be rewarding! Albeit we only practiced for 15 minutes before we had to leave, it seemed promising for a second. I tried to have him stay seated, us getting closer to him and the treat, redirecting Mary's attention each time we sat after getting closer. There were a couple instances she barked and paid close attention to him, and then eventually happily took the peanut butter, but once he re-centered her focus, the peanut butter did not matter one bit. I was holding her on the leash but she tried to lunge at him again, barking non-stop until he was out of sight. **The big instance was my father in law. Granted we warned him not to get too close to her because of the issues with males, but nevertheless he stuck the back of his hand out for her to sniff (I was still trying to be cautious and hold her back), but sure enough she lunged at him and barked aggressively as I pulled her away to keep her from everyone. She had nipped him, superficially, but got some skin. He was fine and got the necessary care (mad/upset in the moment but he understood that she had some issues), but had this been a member of the public and someone we didn't know, it would not have been 'fine' and Mary may not have had another chance.After profusely apologizing on her behalf, I was so sad and defeated at that moment from all the culminating events. I knew she needed help to address her triggers and trauma because this behavior was unacceptable, and I was equally sad that whatever the instance was, that she had suffered/endured pain at the hands of a man who has now instilled this response in her... ***On walks I try to redirect her attention away from males or switch directions. Sometimes she catches on though or passing a man is unavoidable, in this case, she will pull on her leash and bark at them, never close enough to get to the public. I've worked on saying no, her name, go, she is great with those commands but once we come into male contact she is far less receptive to those words without a tug on her leash. I had also initially thought she was dog reactive. And while there can be some dogs she barks at, even with a female handler, she has had really positive experiences being excited to meet other dogs, and especially with an older, very well-trained/behaved pit-mix that belongs to the upstairs neighbor. They sniff each other, wag their tails happily, neither bark at each other, looking forward to seeing her when she passes by our window/porch - Mary seems to know to respect the dog rules between them. Even when in contact with the male owner (40's), Mary didn't seem to have an issue (perhaps because the other dog was protecting him and she knew to back off). ****Yesterday we were returning from a walk around our apartment complex and we encountered this same neighbor and his dog. The dogs were happy to see each other and even the owner of the other dog was able to pet Mary/touch her snout, without issue. We spent 20 minutes talking, describing Mary's history, asking for advice since his dog was also a pit-mix that he rescued some years ago from the shelter. Then as they were leaving and he passed us between two cars, Mary tried to go at him and barked, she didn't get near him as I had a tight grip but then we started thinking maybe she is especially triggered when she feels cornered/in a tight space with a man... ****We talked for another 5 minutes. One final time the other owner tried to let her sniff the back of his hand to show her it was all okay, and she lunged and tried to nip at him. She did not break skin or anything like that, but did nose his hand like she was trying to bite. He said in this time he noticed her eyes go from normal to a trance-like state, like she wasn't really all there and the trauma was just flooding back to her to cause her to suddenly snap. Unlike the other instances with my family, she did not continue barking in his presence for the few moments we stayed to say goodbye. This is the one thing that is an 'issue', she is genuinely such a loveable, sweet, cuddly, cute, well-behaved (outside of these circumstances) pup that would do great in a home. She would be an amazing addition to anyone's family, as soon as this male-reactivity is worked on. 4/2/2024 Spoke with foster Ashley about tips to socialize Tiny safely.  Here is recap. Go slow.  If you put it on and she fights it, take it off quickly and slowly build up.  Some don’t mind it, others may take more time to adjust.  Socialize her when you can.  I like small pet stores and Home Depot plant nursery when they aren’t busy.  Tell people you are in training.  If you have a patient adult, give them a few treats to toss to her.  If she takes them great.  Either way, thank them and turn around and walk the other way. I have a great pet supermarket. First we’d just go in and walk the store and leave.  Then give staff a small bag of treats to toss.  They typically understand your goal is to socialize. Invite a few friends over.  Have them stand in a circle, line or whatever space allows.  Have them toss treats. Don’t look at her, talk to her, face sideways vs directly looking at her.  Sometimes that can make a pup nervous and can cause reactions. Over time, build up and see if she will take treats from them but not in same session.  If you have people over and can, gate her away but let her see / hear what’s going on.  If she hangs out at gate, have them toss her treats.  Over time, if she wants to join, let her do that but help her on a leash so you can move her if needed. Let her decide if she wants to engage.  Also sent body language docs and body language ladder.  cheryl Scheck

7/12/2024 Today we wanted to discuss Leash Reactivity, and potty training:There are two main reasons why dogs display leash reactivity: fear or frustration. A fearful dog wants to get away from the thing he’s afraid of, so he displays distance-increasing body language, such as snarling and growling. It’s his way of saying, “Hey, you! You make me uncomfortable! Stay away from me!” A frustrated dog, on the other hand, displays distance decreasing body language, such as playful barking and bounciness. It’s his way of saying, “Hey, you look fun! Come meet me!”The first step in working with your dog’s reactivity is to determine the underlying cause behind the behavior through his body language. Is he fearful or frustrated? The answer to that question can shape the behavior modification approach you use.Threshold resource attached. I asked if the man could come into the yard before we started the meet and greet to determine if she was going to be okay with him. She was originally panting from the heat but switched to a stress pant and worried eyebrows. She walked with me on leash by him a few times and she completely ignored him, turning her back to him and trying to avoid making contact with him. I asked him to approach her carefully and she continued to ignore him. He reached out slowly to pet her and she sniffed his hand, licked his fingers briefly before stiffening. I pulled the leash back at the same time she started alarm barking at him. We determined it wasn’t a good fit and did not continue with the dog test. There were two women yelling in the hallway about how cute a dog was when we were coming back in, spooking Pharadise and causing her to back up and alarm bark at them when they tried to rush and pet her. I advised she was nervous and they understood and stepped back. There was also a man standing behind them. I walked her into the 80s and Lamar was standing nearby. I tried to tell him to give me some space to put her back but he kept approaching saying she was fine with him but each time he got closer she leaned further and further away, her eyes getting wider. He wasn’t picking up on her body language so I stepped between her and him and told him to please give  her time to decompress. I’m not sure if she actually is okay being handled by him or just tolerates it. He came behind while I was unleashing her and she low growled. Pharadise has some minimal general anxiety but clearly has some aversion/distrust of men. (Could be contributed to 2/3 men not recognizing her signs of stress and continuing to try and interact with her).

She is soooo friendly and loves snuggles and bringing her toys to show them off when she sees us first thing. she doesn’t bark at all except when she saw one of my cats. She greeted my 13 year old son wonderfully after arriving to the house for the first time. She greeted my 11 year old daughter arriving home no problems later that evening for the first time, grabbing her plushie to show her with excitement. and she also greeted my husband this morning, who she hadn’t met yet, when he arrived home from working over night. she was excited to welcome him as a new person into the home. Goes potty outside easily. Went to bed happily last night and after I took out to go pee around 1am, she went back to bed like she knew the routine already. She is absolutely wonderful!! 🥰  A few things that have me concerned though. It seems being in a creat aggravates her back knees. She is well behaved in a creat so that’s not an issue. But I actually have only had her in the creat a few times because of obvious discomfort when getting out even after a short time (lass than an hour), and the fact she has been great hanging out downstairs or in my son’s room when he is in there. That’s where she slept last night. I think the stairs in our house might aggravate her knees as well. I was told she needs surgery on both back knees at some point soon.  I had kept my cats in my bedroom until half way through the night. Until my older cat insisted on being let out. Simply because Jean seems to come out of her creat stiff and limping even after a short time I let her sleep uncreated. I was worried my son would walk out to go toilet during the night and she would get out and neither her nor my cats are ready to meet face to face.  my cats are not happy staying confined to my bedroom. I’ve started to leash Jean to bring her out of my sons room for potty breaks, seen my cats are back to freely moving around the house. which she is fine with, but she seems overly interested in the cats as I take her outside. Over time I’m sure this would ease off. Seen she seems in pain from being in her creat, I am not sure I feel comfortable leaving her in my son’s bedroom uncreated with the door shut without someone in there with her. This will be a problem when I need to go out and leave her home without someone here. I don’t think she Would need to be created for the most part to transition into a new home because she is so wonderful. But because of my cats I think the process is going to be difficult  with the creat and her being in pain. My older cat will transition fast, as she has been around dogs before,  but it seems the younger two are not taking it so well. It will be a longer process.  Another concern is my son was getting a rash and itching. He has asthma and has been allergy tested for dogs when he was younger and it was negative. But this seems to have changed. Our last pup was a pultipoo, so being hypoallergenic he didn’t have an issue. He takes an allergy pill every day but I had to give him Benadryl last night.  Jean is so wonderful and I know she would make a wonderful addition to a family! She is so easy to have in the home, minus the cat introduction process and her being in pain with being in a creat.

Bobo eats 3 meals a day to try and gain a little weight - each one about 1 cup of kibble. 

He got a steroid shot for his allergies last Friday (8/18). The shot will last one week to help stop the itching. On this Friday (8/25) he will start the steroid pills (smaller pill bottle with big white pills) to finish out the allergy treatment. He will get one every 48 hours until the bottle runs out. 

The steroids make him super thirsty and he needs to pee more often. I’ve been giving him lots of water in the morning and early afternoon and taking him out to pee every few hours. I stop giving him water around 4/5 PM and then take him out to pee right before bed. He can usually last through the night without an accident in his crate. 

Before he was on steroids, I let him sleep out in the living room, but I’ve been keeping him in the crate at night since he’s been on meds to try and make sure he doesn’t have an accident when I’m asleep. He doesn’t mind the crate once you give him a gentle push inside. 

When I’m gone, I have been leaving him to roam in my living room. He chewed up one coaster when he was feeling naughty, but otherwise he just naps or wanders around (I watch him on my doggy camera). I have been giving him a kong with peanut butter when I leave which he really loves. 

He’s learning how to use toys and go for walks, so he’s a work in progress! He doesn’t really pull on a leash - if anything I am dragging him along to stop him from sniffing so much. He probably won’t need many walks at all if you guys have a big backyard! Bobo is definitely not a high energy dog. He just needs lots of loving <3

So far, Bobo has shown 0 aggression. He does not resource guard and has been very friendly of all people and dogs we’ve met out and about. Other dogs are sometimes wary of him since he isn’t neutered, but many have warmed up to him after they realize he just wants to sniff their butt. He doesn’t hump other dogs but he does sometimes hump me, so just firmly push him off and say NO super loudly. He usually gets the picture lol. 

His neuter is on 9/7 and they want you to drop him off the night before and pick him up at the end of the day. I can help with drop off and pick up since I’m only 10 minutes away from the shelter if you need it!

He needs to be neutered ASAP so other dogs give him a chance and more people could be potential adopters/fosterers. He LOVES other dogs, they just don’t love him.
